**Analyzing follow-ups and adjustments**

I’m noting down key analyses like single-trial decoding, mixed-effects models, spectral analyses, and more. For feasible follow-ups, I could suggest adding attentional-cue blocks and pupilometry if the user wants. rounds.response: Below are six concrete, testable mechanistic hypotheses linking identifiable neural signatures to individual- and session-level WM variability; each includes the core expected pattern and one clear discriminant alternative and is directly testable with MUA/LFP, behavior, and standard analyses. 1) Persistent spiking stability: higher accuracy/speed will co-occur with larger stimulus-selective, elevated delay-period MUA in PFC (greater firing-rate separation between held vs. non-held items) and single-trial MUA magnitude should predict trial outcome; discriminate from global arousal by controlling for pupil/RT and showing the effect is stimulus-selective and remains after removing arousal-related variance. 2) Transient burst coding: better performance is associated with more frequent high-frequency MUA bursts that are phase-locked to theta during the delay (higher burst rate and theta-locking), with information decodable from burst-timed windows but not from time-averaged rates; discriminate from persistent-rate accounts by showing bursts explain unique variance in behavior when mean rate is regressed out. 3) PFC–parietal theta-phase coupling: sessions/subjects with stronger PFC↔parietal theta phase-locking and increased PFC spike-phase consistency to parietal theta will perform better; discriminate from common-input/arousal by testing directionality (lead–lag, Granger/transfer entropy) and by showing coupling predicts behavior beyond local power. 4) Cross-frequency coupling for precision: greater theta–gamma PAC within PFC and between PFC/parietal during maintenance predicts higher accuracy and faster RTs; discriminate from nonspecific power effects by demonstrating PAC explains behavioral variance beyond theta and gamma power in regression models. 5) Dynamic attractor stability: lower behavioral variability/session stability maps onto more stable, separable low-dimensional delay-period trajectories in PFC state-space (reduced within-trial drift and greater between-item separability) and higher decoding generalization across delay timepoints; discriminate from input variability by residualizing sensory-evoked trial variability and showing state-space metrics still predict behavior. 6) Pre-trial network state bias: single-trial pre-stimulus LFP features (e.g., lower alpha, higher PFC–parietal connectivity) will predict subsequent encoding strength and trial success; discriminate from slow session trends by demonstrating within-session, trial-by-trial predictive power after including session-level covariates. Key suggested analyses: single-trial decoding/regression (cross-validated), mixed-effects models linking neural metrics to behavior across sessions/subjects, spectral and spike–LFP coupling measures, directed connectivity (Granger/TE), and low-dimensional trajectory analyses (PCA/dPCA); feasible, low-cost follow-ups include adding pupilometry and brief attentional-cue blocks to help dissociate arousal vs. mechanism. Suggested minor adjustment (optional): explicitly add arousal/excitability control regressors (pupil, baseline RT, pre-trial power) to the analysis plan to sharpen discrimination between mechanistic hypotheses—if accepted I will prioritize scripts for hypotheses 1–3 before tomorrow’s meeting.

1) Persistent spiking stability — (a) Hypothesis: greater stimulus-selective PFC delay-period firing-rate separation predicts higher trial accuracy and faster RTs; (b) Analysis: fit mixed-effects models (logistic for accuracy, linear for RT) with trial-level predictor = preferred−non-preferred delay firing-rate separation and random intercepts for subject/session; (c) Alternative: global arousal/non-specific excitability; distinguish by adding arousal covariates (pre-trial spectral power, baseline RT) and mean firing-rate to the model and showing the selective separation effect remains (Note: arousal proxies in current data are limited to spectral/RT, no pupil).  
2) Transient burst coding — (a) Hypothesis: higher rate of high-frequency MUA bursts during the delay, and stronger burst–theta phase-locking, predict better accuracy and faster RTs; (b) Analysis: regress behavior on trial-level burst rate and burst–theta PLV while controlling for mean delay firing-rate and compare explanatory power to models using time-averaged rates and to decoding performance from burst-timed windows vs. whole-delay averages; (c) Alternative: persistent-rate coding explains behavior; distinguish by showing burst metrics and burst-timed decoders explain unique variance beyond mean-rate models.  
3) PFC–parietal theta-phase coupling — (a) Hypothesis: stronger PFC↔parietal theta phase-locking and higher PFC spike-phase consistency to parietal theta predict higher accuracy and faster RTs across sessions/subjects; (b) Analysis: mixed-effects regressions using trial/session PLV and spike–phase-locking as predictors and include directed-connectivity measures (Granger/transfer entropy) to test lead–lag; (c) Alternative: coupling reflects common-input/arousal; distinguish by demonstrating directional lead–lag and that coupling predicts behavior above and beyond local power and arousal covariates.  
4) Dynamic attractor stability — (a) Hypothesis: sessions/subjects with more stable, separable low-dimensional PFC delay trajectories (lower within-trial drift, higher between-item separability, and greater time-generalization decoding) show higher accuracy and lower RT variability; (b) Analysis: compute trajectory metrics (PCA/dPCA drift and separability, time-generalized decoder accuracy) per trial/session and regress behavioral metrics on these while controlling for sensory-evoked variability; (c) Alternative: behavioral differences driven by input/sensory encoding variability; distinguish by residualizing sensory-evoked responses (early-evoked firing) and showing state-space stability still predicts behavior.

rounds.response:
1) Model 1 — In plain language: we will fit hierarchical (subject/session) models that predict trial-by-trial accuracy and reaction time from a PFC persistent-selectivity metric (difference in delay activity for held vs. non-held items), PFC beta-burst rate during the delay, and baseline mean firing-rate, with grouped arousal covariates (previous-trial RT and pre-trial spectral power) included; evidence for stabilized persistent PFC activity is a reliable, sizable improvement in prediction driven by the persistent-selectivity predictor (large coefficient/odds-ratio and meaningful ΔR2/ΔAUC when added to baseline), evidence for beta-burst disengagement is a parallel improvement driven instead by beta-burst rate, and a simpler/arousal-only baseline is favored if neither neural predictor adds beyond mean-rate/RT history or if effects vanish after adding arousal covariates; key robustness checks to report are predictor collinearity diagnostics and variance inflation factors, results from orthogonalizing selectivity vs mean-rate, bootstrap/CIs for coefficients, sensitivity to using Poisson/zero-inflated models for burst counts, and how effect sizes change when arousal covariates are included.  
2) Model 2 — In plain language: we will perform nested model comparisons and cross-validated prediction tests that compare a baseline model (mean firing-rate + RT history) to versions that add (A) persistent-selectivity and (B) beta-burst feature sets, and we will also compare decoders trained on whole-delay mean-rate windows versus burst-timed windows; evidence favoring persistent-activity is larger out-of-sample gains and better time-generalization from mean-rate/selectivity features, evidence favoring burst-based disengagement is larger gains from burst features and superior decoding when aligned to bursts, and an arousal-only account is supported if adding either neural feature set fails to improve out-of-sample prediction beyond models with RT-history and pre-trial spectral covariates; key diagnostics are nested cross-validation with permutation baselines, reporting AUC/RMSE differences with confidence intervals, checking class balance and decoder calibration, and showing how predicted gains change when arousal covariates are added.  
3) Integrative summary — Taken together, consistency across models in which predictor set (persistent-selectivity vs. beta-burst features) provides the largest unique and out-of-sample explanatory power will argue for stabilized persistent activity versus burst-linked disengagement, whereas systematic attenuation of these neural effects after adding arousal covariates would point to an arousal-centered explanation; collaborators should note the important limitation that our arousal measures are indirect (spectral power and RT history only, no pupil), so where effects attenuate with these covariates we will report that as evidence suggestive but not definitive of arousal mediation.
